title: Ὁ Λόγος
summary: Read the alphabet, meet the ten most common words in the New Testament, learn 'to be' and 'the', and read John 1:1–2 in Greek.

rule.title: Twenty-four letters
rule.body: Greek has 24 letters; you already know several from math and science (α β γ δ π). Learn each letter's name, its lowercase shape, and its sound. Capitals are used only at the start of names and paragraphs, so lowercase matters most.

rule.title: The second half
rule.body: Watch the look-alikes: ν (nu) is not v, ρ (rho) is not p, and χ (chi) is not x. Sigma has two shapes: σ inside a word, ς at the end (θεός).

rule.title: Two vowels, one sound
rule.body: Seven vowels (α ε η ι ο υ ω) combine into diphthongs that are read as one syllable. Every word beginning with a vowel wears a breathing mark: rough ( ῾ ) adds an h-sound, smooth ( ᾿ ) adds nothing.

examples.en: en ar-chay: in [the] beginning (the ῃ hides an iota)

rule.title: Stress the accented syllable
rule.body: Three accent marks, one job for a reader: they show which syllable to stress. Punctuation is mostly familiar, with two traps: the raised dot (·) is a semicolon/colon, and the Greek question mark looks exactly like our semicolon (;).

examples.gr: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν
examples.en: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God

lessons.label: καί
lessons.sub: The ten most common little words

rule.title: Words that never change
rule.body: Conjunctions, prepositions and the negatives have no endings to learn, and these ten alone are about one word in every seven in the New Testament. οὐ is 'not' for facts (indicative); μή is 'not' for everything else (commands, wishes, conditions).

vocab.gloss: but, on the other hand, and

vocab.citation: ἐκ, before vowels ἐξ, prep. w. gen., introducing various aspects of separation or derivation (opp. εἰς, which is goal- oriented) – a. relating in general to a matter of origin; resources of English encourage a variety of glosses – α. of place or thing, from, out of (the latter gloss usually preferred where focus is on movement or removal) Mt 2:6, 15; 3:9; 7:4; 8:28 (explicitly opp. εἰς); 17:5; 26:27 (of taking a drink out of a cup); in related mode 1 Cor 9:13 (ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἐσθίειν =eat of things derived from the temple); of material source Mt 27:29 (a wreath
vocab.gloss: from out, out from among, from

lessons.label: εἰμί
lessons.sub: To be, and the words of John 1:1

rule.title: Verbs carry their subject
rule.body: A Greek verb ending tells you who is doing it, so 'I am' is one word: εἰμί. ἐστίν = 'he/she/it is', εἰσίν = 'they are'. There is usually no separate word for 'I', 'you' or 'he' unless the writer wants emphasis.

examples.gr: ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου
examples.en: you are the light of the world

vocab.gloss: a word, speech, divine utterance, analogy
a man, one of the human race

lessons.label: ὁ ἡ τό
lessons.sub: The article and the four cases

rule.title: Endings do the work of word order
rule.body: English uses word order to show who does what; Greek uses endings called cases. Nominative = subject (ὁ λόγος), genitive = 'of' (τοῦ θεοῦ), dative = 'to / for / in' (τῷ θεῷ), accusative = object (τὸν λόγον). The article (the) changes with its noun and is your best clue to the case.

examples.gr: ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν
examples.en: the Word was with God (ὁ = subject, τόν = after the preposition)

vocab.citation: ὁ, ἡ, τό; pl. οἱ, αἱ, τά

vocab.gloss: he, she, it, they, them, same
as, like as, how, while, so that

rule.title: Read for meaning
rule.body: You already know almost every word here. Read the Greek, form the sense in your head, then reveal the translation and rate yourself honestly. Tap any word you do not know for its gloss; those taps are how the app learns what to teach you next.
